Divergence only tells you "**This section is not strong enough**", but it **cannot determine** how the price will move next - this is why there will be more than one way to move after Divergence.

## 2. Evolution 1: Reversal

After **Divergence, the price really turned** - it turned to increase after falling Divergence, and then turned to fall after rising Divergence, creating a **turning** at this level (the corresponding type 1 buying and selling point was realized).

This is the situation that everyone is most looking forward to, and it is also the source of the misunderstanding "Divergence = reversal". But please note: **Reversal is only one of three evolutions** and is not an inevitable result. Treating it as the only possibility is the beginning of losses.

## 3. Evolution 2: Consolidation (Transfer to Central Hub/Consolidation)

After **Divergence, the price did not reverse significantly, but entered a period of consolidation** - it stayed sideways.

This corresponds to the theorem C1-3: **Divergence of a certain level of trend will cause the level of the last Central Hub of the trend to expand** and evolve into **a larger level of consolidation** (or a higher level counter-trend). The specific manifestation is: the price does not turn around and fall / rise sharply after Divergence, but enters a range and goes back and forth (forming a new Central Hub, or an expansion and upgrade of the original Central Hub, see C1-2).

This situation is very common, but it is most easily ignored - many people think that "Divergence either reverses or continues", forgetting that "sideways consolidation" is the most likely intermediate state**.

## 4. Evolution 3: Continue (Divergence passivation/failure)

**After Divergence, the price just pauses for a moment and then continues in the original direction** - that is, "**Divergence passivation/Divergence failure**".

It is especially common in **strong trends**: MACD seems to be divergent (the column area shrinks, the yellow and white lines pull back), but the price increases again and continues to hit new highs/new lows. At this time, if you enter the market against the trend because you "see Divergence", you will be severely slapped in the face by the continuing trend.

**Divergence will be passivated** - this point has been repeatedly emphasized in C1-7 and C1-13, and it is nailed down again: **Don't take the "appearance of Divergence" as "the inevitable end of the trend". **

Fundamental reason: **Divergence only describes "this period of strength exhaustion", but how the market goes next depends on greater levels of power, new funds, the overall environment, etc. - these are not determined by "this period of Divergence". **

Therefore, what Divergence provides is a "signal light of exhaustion" rather than a script of "what will happen next". The correct usage is to understand it as a probabilistic reference (C1-20), rather than a deterministic switch.

These three evolutions give three direct reminders for actual combat:

2. - **3 buy invalid**: After the 3 buy, the pullback **falls back to the Central Hub range (breaking ZG)** - indicating that the upward breakthrough has not been established, and this 3 buy is not established (it is likely to evolve into an extension/expansion of Central Hub, see C1-2).

> Midas Academy · Chan Theory Advanced · Structure Advanced

In the introduction, Central Hub is "the interval where at least three sub-level trends overlap." ## 1. First, nail down the two sets of boundaries of Central Hub (this is the basis for distinction)

To clearly explain extension and expansion, we must first distinguish the **two groups** of key price points of Central Hub. Many people get confused because they don’t make the distinction here:

- **Central Hub range (ZG ~ ZD)**: This is the "strict sense" range of Central Hub.
  - **ZG (Central Hub upper edge) = the "minimum value" of the high point of each segment in the first three segments that constitute the Central Hub**;
  - **ZD (Central Hub lower edge) = the "maximum value" of the low point of each segment in the first three segments**.
  - (That is, take the lowest of the three high points as the upper edge, and the highest of the three low points as the lower edge - this is the area where the three periods truly "overlap", be sure not to invert it.)
- **Swing Range (GG ~ DD)**: This is the "maximum envelope" of price fluctuations during Central Hub.
  - **GG = the maximum value of all high points in Central Hub**;
  - **DD = the minimum value of all lows in the Central Hub**.

**ZG~ZD is the "core overlap area" (small), GG~DD is the "fluctuation outer frame" (large)**. The difference between extension, expansion, and expansion lies precisely in "which set of intervals you return to."

![C1-2 with picture 1](/academy-img/C1-2-配图1.png)

## 2. Central Hub extension: Three Types of Buy and Sell Points are not released, and the Central Hub is repeated.

**Extension means that after the Central Hub is formed, the trend does not appear, but continues to move back and forth around the Central Hub range. **

The characteristics are:

- **Premise**: **No** Three Types of Buy and Sell Points appear (the trend does not really "leave and stand firm" Central Hub);
- **Performance**: The sub-level trend shuttles back and forth in the Central Hub range segment by segment, and the "number of segments" of the Central Hub continues to increase - segment 3 is the initial composition, and it may be segment 5, segment 7, segment 9... in the future;
- **Scope**: During the extension process, the Central Hub range** is still mainly determined by the initial first three segments** (ZG/ZD remains unchanged);
- **Upgrade point**: When extended to **Segment 9**, this Central Hub will be **upgraded** to a higher level Central Hub (in Chan Theory, the Central Hub level is pushed forward by the power of 3; Segments 5 and 7 are just extensions, not upgraded, and will not be upgraded until Segment 9).

![C1-2 with picture 2](/academy-img/C1-2-配图2.png)

## 3. Central Hub Extension: Three Types of Buy and Sell Points are out, but "back"

**Expansion means that after the formation of Central Hub, the trend went out of the (sub-level) Three Types of Buy and Sell Points. The original Central Hub was once considered to be over, but then the trend of leaving "returned to the original Central Hub range (ZG ~ ZD)". **

Looking at the extension, there are two key differences:

- **Different premise**: The extension is **appeared** Three Types of Buy and Sell Points (the extension is not out). The Three Types of Buy and Sell Points means that "Central Hub was once settled and the trend tried to leave";
- **Extent of return**: After leaving, the trend** returned to the core Central Hub range of ZG~ZD** (note: the expansion looks at ZG and ZD, not GG and DD).

The result is: you will see that the two Central Hub intervals overlap/entangle, so they are "expanded" and merged, which brings about the upgrade of this level of Central Hub (to a higher level Central Hub).

One sentence to remember: **Expansion = Three transactions occurred, the transaction returned to the original Central Hub range (ZG~ZD), and the two Central Hubs were upgraded overlappingly. **

![C1-2 with picture 3](/academy-img/C1-2-配图3.png)

## 4. Let’s clarify “expansion (semi-expansion)” by the way: only return to the shock range

There is also a close relative that is often confused with expansion - **expansion (also called semi-expansion)**:

**Expansion = After the Three Types of Buy and Sell Points appear and the trend leaves, the pullback only returns to the original Central Hub's "oscillating range (GG ~ DD)", but does not return to the "Central Hub range (ZG ~ ZD)". **

So to distinguish between expansion and expansion, just one sentence: **Which range does the pullback after the Three Types of Buy and Sell Points return to? **

- Returned to the **Central Hub interval ZG~ZD** → **Extended**;
- Only returned to the **shock range GG~DD** and did not enter ZG~ZD → **expansion (semi-expansion)**.

Two additional points: Expansion and expansion will both cause the Central Hub to be upgraded (to a higher-level Central Hub), but in different forms; and in practice, you can "expand first and then expand", but you cannot "expand first and then expand".

![C1-2 with picture 4](/academy-img/C1-2-配图4.png)

## 5. How can "extension" and "expansion" be distinguished at a glance?

Condensate the core judgments into a decision-making logic, and ask yourself this in actual combat:

1. **Does Three Types of Buy and Sell Points appear? **
   - **No** → The trend repeats in the Central Hub → **Extend** (upgrade at 9 levels);
   - **Yes** → Go to question 2.
2. Where did the pullback after **Three Types of Buy and Sell Points return? **
   - Return to **ZG~ZD (Central Hub interval)** → **Extended**;
   - Only returns to **GG~DD (oscillatory range)** → **Expansion (semi-expansion)**.

# Thinking in Probabilities with Chan Theory

> Midas Academy · Chan Theory Advanced · Advanced Special Topics

After learning this, you must establish the **most important cognition** - what Chan Theory gives you is "**structure and probability**", not "**inevitability and prediction**". This article talks about how to look at Chan Theory from a **probabilistic perspective**. It is the "heart-warming" chapter of the entire C1 advancement, and also echoes the mentality and long-termism discussed by Group F.

**Quick overview of this article**

- What Chan Theory gives is **structure and probability**, **not necessity and prediction**; it helps you objectively describe "where the structure has gone", but "the structure has reached a certain position" only means "a certain move has a higher probability", not necessarily.
- The buying and selling points will fail, Divergence has three evolutions, the trend has multiple meanings, and the boundaries are entangled with thousands of people - all of this shows that **Chan Theory is a probability framework, not a fortune-telling machine**.
- "Inevitability" does not exist: The market is full of uncertainties, and no framework can eliminate uncertainties and can only find probabilistic advantages; claiming that "Chan Theory must be accurate" is a myth.
- Four key points of probabilistic thinking: **Improving the odds of winning is not about pursuing certainty, always being prepared for misreading (Stop Loss/Risk Control), relying on repeated repetitions to make the probability manifest in the long term, and being right about things but not about the results**.
- **Probabilistic thinking vs. Gambler's thinking**: The former admits and manages uncertainty and relies on long-term probability and compound interest; the latter denies uncertainty, bets on certainty, and doubles losses.
- ⚠️ Chan Theory is an **analysis framework/probabilistic reference**. It does not predict, guarantee, or deify; it can only be used with probabilistic thinking and awe.

## 1. Chan Theory is not "fortune telling", but a "structural probability framework"

Many people learn Chan Theory for the purpose of "whether they can calculate every stroke accurately." This was wrong from the start.

- The strength of Chan Theory is that it **strictly defines the trend structure** (Stroke / Segment / Central Hub / Level / Buying and Selling Point), allowing you to **objectively describe "where the structure has gone now"**;
- But "the structure reaches a certain position" only means "the probability of a certain move next is relatively higher", and it does not mean "it must move this way"**.

Many of the things we have talked about along the way are actually saying the same thing over and over again: **Chan Theory gives probability, not certainty**——

- **The buying and selling point will fail** (C1-19);
- **There are three kinds of evolution after Divergence** (C1-18), Divergence is not necessarily reversed;

- **Trend**: divided into **rising** and **falling**;
- **Consolidation**.

Just these two categories, there is no third one. The standard for distinguishing them is not something vague like "how much it has increased" or "how big the slope is", but a very hard indicator - **This trend includes several Central Hubs (of this level). **

## 2. Consolidation: Only one Central Hub is included

**Definition of consolidation: A certain level of Trend Type contains only one Central Hub of that level. **

There is only one Central Hub, which means that the long and short forces repeatedly see-saw in a range and there is no directional "relay". It corresponds to "shocks and sideways" in our intuition, but Chan Theory gives it a countable hard standard: **Central Hub quantity = 1**.

- **At least two Central Hubs**: One Central Hub is consolidation, **two or more** may be a trend;
- **Same direction in turn**: These Central Hubs must "relay" in the same direction——
  - **Uptrend**: The range of the next Central Hub is overall **higher than** the previous Central Hub (Central Hub moves upward step by step);
  - **Downward trend**: The range of the next Central Hub is overall **lower than** the previous Central Hub (Central Hub is falling step by step).

Intuitive understanding: Trend = **"Central Hub + the trend of connecting Central Hub + another higher/lower Central Hub"**. The price does not stay in a range, but **walks out of a range and rushes to a higher (or lower) range**. This "Central Hub relay" is the essence of the trend.

The advantage of Chan Theory's "Central Hub" is that it turns "trend/consolidation" into a **structured and reviewable** judgment:

- It does not ask "whether the rise is steep or not", but only asks "whether you have exited the second and third Central Hub in the same direction";
- For a trend that seems to have risen a lot, if ** always repeats ** in only one Central Hub (even if the amplitude is large), Chan Theory will judge it as **consolidation**, not a trend;

This is a more subtle move. Compare the MACD pillars corresponding to the two adjacent periods of the same trend in the trend to the "**area**":

- Use **red bars** for increases (DIF is above DEA), and **green bars** for decreases;
- Top Divergence: The price hit a new high in the last period, but the corresponding ** red column area is significantly smaller than the previous period** - the intensity is shrinking, Divergence;
- Bottom Divergence: The price hit a new low in the last period, but the corresponding green column area was significantly smaller than the previous period - Divergence.

- The core structure is from small to large: **Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub**, and has the characteristics of **level recursion**.
- Compared with traditional technical analysis, Chan Theory emphasizes **geometric structure, complete classification (trend/consolidation), and level recursion**.
- Chan Theory** has a huge system, has a learning threshold**, and is an **analysis tool rather than a prediction tool** - it is not deified and does not promise guaranteed profits.

## 1. Concept introduction: from "looking at indicators" to "looking at structure"

After learning this, you have already learned about moving average, MACD, Bollinger Bands, RSI and other technical indicators. Most of them "superimpose a calculated value on the price" to assist judgment. And **Chan Theory** provides a very different perspective: it does not rely on a certain indicator, but **uses a strict geometric structure to dismantle and describe the price trend itself layer by layer**.

Chan Theory is a very influential and controversial analysis system in the Chinese trading circle. It has a large system and self-consistent logic, but it also has a high learning threshold. This article will first explain clearly: what Chan Theory is, where it comes from, and how it is different from ordinary technical analysis.

## 2. Source of Chan Theory

Chan Theory originated from an online serial: a series of articles published on the blog by the author under the name of Stroke **"Zhongzhongshuochan"** (the part about trading is often called the "Teaching You to Trade in Stocks" series). These articles were later compiled by readers and collectively referred to as "Chan Theory".

It should be noted that: **"Chen Theory" is the author's Stroke name**, and Chan Theory was originally published in the form of an online blog series. This training camp introduces the core concepts of the analysis method itself and does not involve the verification of the author's identity.

## 3. The core concept of Chan Theory: using geometric structures to decompose trends

The core feature of Chan Theory is to decompose the chaotic price trends into a set of progressive geometric structural units**. From small to large, the relationship is roughly as follows:

**Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub**

- **Fractal**: The minimum turning structure composed of three (processed) K lines, marking the local top or bottom.
- **Stroke**: Connects an adjacent Top Fractal and a Bottom Fractal, which is the most basic trend unit.
- **Segment**: A higher-level trend composed of several Strokes (at least three Strokes).
- **Central Hub**: It is composed of overlapping intervals of three consecutive trends. It is a very core concept in Chan Theory.

(Let’s establish the overall impression here first. The precise definitions of Fractal, Stroke, Segment, and Central Hub will be expanded one by one in the following articles.)

![C1 with picture 1](/academy-img/C1-配图1.png)

This set of structures has an important feature - **level recursion**: the same structure (Fractal, Stroke, Central Hub...) will **reappear** at different time levels. The combination of small-level structures into large-level structures is like building the same building blocks repeatedly on different scales. This allows Chan Theory to use the same language to describe trends at multiple levels.

## 4. How is it different from ordinary technical analysis?

Chan Theory and the technical indicators we learned earlier have very different ideas:

- **Traditional technical analysis**: relies more on **indicators** (Moving Average, MACD, RSI, etc.) and **classic forms**, with strong statistical and empirical color.
- **Chan Theory**: Emphasizes the use of **strict geometric structures** to describe trends, and pursues a goal called **"complete classification"** - that is, trying to exhaustively classify all possible trends into a limited number of types (the core are the two categories of "trend" and "consolidation"). In conjunction with level recursion, Chan Theory attempts to give the trend a structured and systematic description framework.

![C1 with picture 2](/academy-img/C1-配图2.png)

To put it simply: traditional indicators are more like "several indicators that conduct a physical examination of prices", while Chan Theory is more like "drawing a complete set of anatomical structure diagrams for prices".

![C1 with picture 3](/academy-img/C1-配图3.png)

## 5. Scope of application and learning difficulty (must be viewed rationally)

As an analysis framework, Chan Theory can theoretically be used in any market with continuous prices and K lines that can be drawn. But there are two points that must be said before:

1. **It has a huge system and a learning threshold. ** Fractal, Stroke, Segment, Central Hub, trend level, Divergence...the concepts are intertwined and need to be understood **step by step** and cannot be expected to be achieved quickly.
2. **It is an analysis tool, not a prediction tool. ** This point is extremely important: Chan Theory can help you **structuredly describe and understand trends**, but it **cannot guarantee predicting the future, let alone profit**. The claims on the market that "you can make sure money by learning Chan Theory/precisely copy the bottom and escape the top" are all exaggerated and misleading.

Regarding "How to treat Chan Theory rationally", the next article will be devoted to it.

- The core structure is from small to large: **Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub**, and has the characteristics of **level recursion**.
- Compared with traditional technical analysis, Chan Theory emphasizes **geometric structure, complete classification (trend/consolidation), and level recursion**.
- Chan Theory** has a huge system, has a learning threshold**, and is an **analysis tool rather than a prediction tool** - it is not deified and does not promise guaranteed profits.

# Using Leverage Appropriately vs. Excessively

> Midas Academy · C2 contract case library (full virtual / indicating market conditions)

Old traders often say: "**Many people lose not in direction, but in leverage.**" In this article, we use a fictitious case to let two people with exactly the same views use different leverage in the same market to see how far the ending can be.

> ⚠️ This article is **fictitious / indicative market conditions and fictitious operations** for teaching purposes. All numbers are indicative. It does not name any real targets, does not predict the real market, and does not constitute buying or selling advice. Contracts are high-risk instruments. This article presents the risks truthfully and does not encourage high leverage.

## 1. Scene setting

- A **symbol of the market**: a fictitious contract, the price starts from **100**, first **normally adjusts to 96**, and then rises all the way to **115**.
- Two traders **A and B**: have exactly the same views - both are bullish, both enter the market at **100**, both plan to wait for an increase, and have similar Stop Loss ideas.
- The only difference: **A uses 3x leverage and B uses 50x leverage. **

The margin for both people is assumed to be 1,000 yuan (A’s exposure is 3,000, B’s exposure is 50,000). Note - their ** direction judgment is the same, and the final direction is also correct ** (the price did rise to 115).

## 2. Operation process

**A (3x leverage):**
- Go Long 100, under 3 times leverage, the **Liquidation price is approximately 100×(1−1/3) ≈ 67** (far away from the position price);
- When the price retraced to 96 - still far away from the Liquidation price of 67, A's position was **unscathed** and could be held;
- The price subsequently rose to 115, and A successfully benefited from this increase.

**B (50x leverage):**
- Same Go Long 100, but under 50 times leverage, the **Liquidation price is approximately 100×(1−1/50) = 98** (including maintenance margin and handling fees, it will actually be earlier, such as 98.x);
- When the price retraces to 96 - **has fallen below B's Liquidation price of 98**! B’s position was directly eliminated by Forced Liquidation and Liquidation;
- When the price rose to 115, B was no longer on the market - he was looking in the right direction, but he didn't make any money and lost all his deposit. **

![C2-1 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-1-配图1.png)

## 3. Dismantling of key nodes

**Node 1: That "normal callback to 96" was a watershed moment. **
A pullback to 96 is a normal fluctuation for this uptrend (there is a pullback in the trend). But **the same callback has two fates for the two levers**: A's Liquidation price of 67 is far away, so the callback cannot affect him; B's Liquidation price of 98 is too close, and the callback directly kicks him out.

**Node 2: The higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation price is to the position price. **
This is the hard truth taught by Group E - **Liquidation price ≈ opening price × (1−1/leverage), long orders are below the opening price; the higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation price is to the opening price** (only 2% difference at 50 times). A 2% fluctuation may only take a few minutes in the contract market. High leverage means compressing one's "fault tolerance space" to almost zero.

**Node 3: Maintenance margin makes actual Liquidation earlier. **
The theoretical Liquidation price of B is 98, but including the maintenance margin rate and handling fees, **the actual liquidation is often triggered a little earlier than 98** - under high leverage, this difference is enough to determine life or death.

![C2-1 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-1-配图2.png)

## 4. Key points of review

The most disturbing part of this case is that **B’s direction judgment was completely correct, but he was eliminated because of excessive use of leverage. **

- **The lever does not change whether your judgment of the direction is right or wrong, it only changes whether you can hold it or not. ** Making the right judgment does not mean making money - you still have to "live" until the market price materializes.
- **High leverage compresses fault tolerance**: A normal callback in the trend is enough for you to liquidate under high leverage. You think that adding leverage is "amplifying profits", but the result is "being eliminated early in normal fluctuations".
- **The other side of "magnifying profits" is always "equally magnifying losses, possibly Liquidation"** - B is a living example.
- Using appropriate leverage (low leverage) is to leave room for error in judgment; using excessive leverage (high leverage) is to leave yourself to luck.

![C2-1 with picture 3](/academy-img/C2-1-配图3.png)

One sentence to end: if the direction is right, you may not win; if the leverage is wrong, you will most likely lose. ** Surviving a long time in a contract is often not because of how accurate your predictions are, but because you don't use excessive leverage**.

## 5. Main points of this article

- Judgment of the same market and the same direction, **low leverage (A) can hold on safely, high leverage (B) Liquidation will be out during a normal callback** - B is in the right direction but loses money.
- **Leverage does not change the direction of judgment, it only changes "whether it can be held"**; the right judgment ≠ makes money, and you have to live until the market cashes out.
- **The higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation price is to the opening price (≈100÷N%, long orders are at the bottom)**, and the maintenance of margin will actually occur earlier; high leverage reduces the fault tolerance space to almost zero.
- ⚠️ The entire process is virtual/signaled; magnifying profits will also magnify losses, and liquidation is possible; high leverage is not encouraged, does not constitute advice, and does not predict.

> Midas Academy · C2 Contract Case Library (Virtual Suggestion Review)

Group E said that "Stop Loss must be set before Liquidation price". This article uses a schematic case to walk through the two paths of "**Set Stop Loss, follow discipline**" and "**Don't Stop Loss, carry orders to Liquidation**" side by side - you will see that if you look in the wrong direction, the ending can be very different**.

- The result was **both misread** - the price did not rise but fell, all the way down;
- The direction judgments of the two people are exactly the same. The only difference is: **C sets Stop Loss and executes it, while D does not set Stop Loss and chooses to carry the order. **

Let's just look at how far this only difference makes the ending.

## 2. Operation process

**C’s approach (by discipline):**

- Before opening a position, use the **1% risk method** (F4) to determine: the maximum loss of this Stroke is **1%** of the total funds. Accordingly, set the **Stop Loss at 95** (leave the market with a 5% drop), and the position should be reversed according to this Stop Loss range;
- The price fell below 95 → C **Without a word, Stop Loss and exit as planned**;
- Result: C lost **1%** of the total capital - a small loss acceptable to Stroke, and the account was almost unscathed.

**D’s approach (taking orders):**

- D **Stop Loss** is not set, and a higher leverage is used (assuming 10 times, the theoretical Liquidation price of long orders is ≈ 100×(1−1/10) = **90**, maintaining margin will actually lead to earlier);
- When the price fell below 95, D thought: "Wait a little longer, it will come back" - **Hold the order but not leave**;

**Node 1: Before opening a position - C has a plan, D has no plan. **

# How Funding Rates Erode Long-term Positions

> Midas Academy · C2 Contract Case Library (Virtual Suggestion Review)

Many people only focus on the rise and fall of prices when making contracts, but forget that Perpetual Contract also has a continuously deducted cost - Funding Rate**. This article uses a schematic case to see how a "long-term holding" contract position can be "gnawed away" by the Funding Rate bit by bit.

> ⚠️ The whole process is virtual/suggestive, the numbers are all assumptions, no real targets are named, no real rates are predicted, and no recommendations are constituted.

## 1. Scene setting (align the mechanism first)

First reiterate the mechanism of Group E (the direction cannot be reversed):

- **Funding Rate** is a mechanism unique to Perpetual Contract, which is collected and paid regularly between **long and short parties (usually settled every few hours, **not a handling fee** paid to the platform);
- **Positive rate: longs pay to shorts; negative rate: shorts pay to longs. **

Setting the scene (made-up numbers):

- The market is in a **positive rate** for a long time (that is, **people who go long will continue to pay people who go short**);
- Trader E is optimistic about the market outlook, **Open Long and intends to hold it for a long time**;
- His ** margin is 1,000 yuan, leverage is 10 times, nominal exposure = 1,000 × 10 = 10,000 yuan**;
- Assume that the average **Funding Rate during this period is about 0.03%/day** (simplified as calculated on a daily basis; in fact, it is settled on a periodic basis, and the rate will fluctuate).

## 2. Operation process

E's idea was simple: "I'm optimistic about it, hold on, and wait for it to rise." So he left it alone after Open Long and held it for 90 days.

But he ignored one thing: **Funding fees are calculated based on "nominal exposure" and are deducted every day. **

- **Daily funding fee = exposure 10,000 × 0.03% = 3 yuan**;
- After holding for **90 days**, the accumulated capital fee = 3 × 90 = **about 270 yuan**;
- And his margin is only **1,000 yuan** - **270 yuan, which is equivalent to 27% of the principal (margin)! **

In other words: **Even if the price remains unchanged and does not increase by a penny during these 90 days**, E has **quietly lost about 27% of its principal** - all eaten up by funding fees. If the price increases only slightly, it may not be enough to cover the capital fee.

![C2-3 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-3-配图1.png)

## 3. Dismantling of key nodes

**Node 1: Funding fees are calculated based on "exposure", not "margin". **
This is the most easily overlooked point. E's margin is only 1,000, but the funding fee is calculated based on an exposure of **10,000** - **Leverage magnifies not only the profit and loss, but also the base of the funding fee**. 10 times leverage means that your capital fee is also paid at 10 times the position.

**Node 2: The longer the time, the more severe the erosion. **
Funding fees are deducted every cycle, like "rent for holding positions". Short-term entry and exit may not be deducted a few times and have little impact; but if you hold it for a long time, it will accumulate over time. The longer you hold it, the more substantial the Stroke "rent" will be.

**Node 3: Under the positive rate, long-term Go Long is a "position against the wind". **
In the long-term **Go Long** in the **positive rate** market, it means **paying money out every day** (longs pay shorts). Even if you are in the right direction, your "profit" must first be deducted from the capital fees paid along the way before you can truly get it. E's fault is not to be bullish, but to hold the position for a long time without including the funding fee.

![C2-3 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-3-配图2.png)

**Node 4: The spot does not have this Stroke cost. **
If E is held for a long time in **spot** (buy and hold currency), there is **no funding fee** (spot defaults to no leverage and no funding fee). This is also an important difference between contracts and spot - the "carrying cost" of contracts is higher than that of spot. For long-term "settled" demand, sometimes spot goods are more worry-free.

# How Liquidation Happens Step by Step

> Midas Academy · C2 Contract Case Library (Virtual Suggestion Review)

Everyone has heard the word "Liquidation", but many people only know it as "losing money". This article uses a schematic case to show you the entire process of a Liquidation from opening a position to liquidation step by step - you will understand that it does not happen suddenly, but is approaching step by step, and why the actual Liquidation is often earlier than the theoretical price you calculated.

> ⚠️ The whole process is virtual/suggestive, and the numbers are all assumptions. It does not name the real targets, does not predict the real market, and does not constitute advice; this article aims to explain the risks clearly and does not encourage high leverage.

## 1. Scene setting

Trader F used **high leverage** Go Long (numerical fiction):

- **Margin 1,000 yuan, leverage 20 times, nominal exposure = 1,000 × 20 = 20,000 yuan**;
- **Opening price 100**, direction Go Long;
- First calculate the two key price points (E group caliber):
  - **Theoretical Liquidation price ≈ 100 × (1 − 1/20) = 95** (that is, if the reverse falls by 5%, the entire margin will be eaten up due to floating losses);
  - But because of the existence of **maintenance margin rate**, **actual liquidation will be triggered earlier than 95** (the price will be liquidated before it falls to 95), we assume that the actual liquidation price ≈ **95.5**.

20 times leverage means that as long as the reverse fluctuation is about 5%, the margin will return to zero - the fault tolerance space is as thin as paper.

## 2. Operation process (approaching Liquidation step by step)

The price did not rise but fell after opening the position. Let's see how F's margin was eaten up one by one (exposure 20,000, every 1% price drop = floating loss 200):

- **Price 100 → 98 (down 2%)**: Floating loss = 20000 × 2% = **400 yuan**, margin remaining 1000 − 400 = **600 yuan**;
- **Price 98 → 96 (down 4% in total)**: Floating loss = **800 yuan**, margin remaining **200 yuan** - already in danger;
- **Price 96 → 95.5 (a total decrease of 4.5%)**: Floating loss ≈ **900 yuan**, the margin remaining is about **100 yuan**, and has **touched the maintenance margin line** → **System Forced Liquidation (Liquidation)**, this Stroke's margin is basically lost.

Note: The price has not yet fallen to the theoretical Liquidation price of 95** (down 5%), but was liquidated at **95.5 (down 4.5%) - this is "actuality is earlier than theory".

![C2-4 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-4-配图1.png)

## 3. Dismantling of key nodes

**Node 1: Why does the leverage of 20 times and the reverse of 5% explode? **
Because Liquidation price ≈ opening price ×(1 − 1/N), the larger N is, the closer it is to the opening price. A reverse fluctuation of 20 times → about (100÷20)% = **5%** will eat up the margin. **The higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation price is to the position price and the smaller the error tolerance** (This is the core of Group E, also mentioned in C2-1). A 5% fluctuation is just "everyday" in many varieties, but it is enough to bring 20 times the position to zero.

**Node 2: Maintenance Margin Rate – Why Reality Comes Earlier Than Theory. **
The exchange requires that your margin cannot be lower than a **maintenance margin** level (a very small percentage). When your remaining margin drops to this maintenance line, the system will force liquidate -- instead of waiting for you to "lose nothing". Therefore, the actual liquidation price (95.5) is triggered earlier than the theoretical Liquidation price (95) of "margin return to zero". Many people calculated based on the theoretical price that they were "a little short of exploding". As a result, they were liquidated in advance. This is where they fell.

![C2-4 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-4-配图2.png)

**Node 3: Liquidation is "approaching", not "sudden". **
From 100 to 98 to 96 to 95.5, F's margin went from 1000 → 600 → 200 → liquidation, which was **eaten step by step**. Every step along the way is actually an opportunity for **Stop Loss to leave the market** - if F falls below a certain preset level (such as 98, or earlier), it will Stop Loss and there will be no Liquidation at all. **Liquidation is not a natural disaster, but the inevitable end of "no Stop Loss along the way". **

**Node 4: Stop Loss could have avoided all of this. **
If F sets the Stop Loss before the Liquidation price (for example, if he leaves the market near 98), he will lose up to 400 and save most of his deposit. **Liquidation = Give up the opportunity of Stop Loss all the way until the system liquidates it for you. ** (Echoes C2-2)

## 4. Key points of review

- **Liquidation = The margin is completely eaten up (nearly eaten up), and the liquidation is forced by the system**; it is **approaching step by step**, not suddenly;
- **High leverage = minimal fault tolerance**: 20 times leverage will return to zero if the reverse direction is about 5% (Liquidation price ≈ opening × (1−1/N), long orders are below, and the larger N, the closer);
- **Actual Liquidation is often earlier than theory**: Because of the **Maintenance Margin Rate** - when the remaining margin touches the maintenance line, it will be liquidated. Don't press "return to zero" to calculate "it's still safe";
- **Every step is an opportunity for Stop Loss**: If you set the Stop Loss before the Liquidation price, you can take the initiative to leave the market halfway and avoid forced liquidation;
- **The root cause of Liquidation is excessive leverage + no Stop Loss**: Lowering leverage and setting up Stop Loss are the two most practical ways to stay away from Liquidation.

![C2-4 with picture 3](/academy-img/C2-4-配图3.png)

One sentence to end: **Liquidation is never a momentary thing, but the result of giving up Stop Loss all the way and giving yourself to leverage. ** Understand how it happens step by step, and you will know where to stop.

## 5. Main points of this article

- Illustrative case: 20 times leverage, margin 1000, exposure 20000, opening position 100; **Theoretical Liquidation 95 (reverse 5%), maintaining margin leads to actual liquidation ≈ 95.5 (earlier)**; price 100→98 (remaining 600)→96 (remaining 200)→95.5 liquidation and loss.
- **The higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation price is to opening a position (≈100÷N%, long orders are at the bottom)**; **Maintain the margin rate → the actual liquidation is earlier than the theory** (don't press "return to zero" to consider it safe).
- Liquidation is **approaching step by step**, and every step in the middle is a **Stop Loss opportunity**; the root cause is **too high leverage + no Stop Loss**.

This article uses a schematic case to see how the losses of "using the wrong strategy in the environment" accumulate.

## 2. Operation process (repeatedly harvested by false breakthroughs)

The operation of G repeats like a repeater:

- ... This was repeated many times, and every time it was "I was beaten back as soon as I chased him in".

Looking at each stroke alone, the loss is not much (the stop loss is very small). But the problem is **more times + additional costs**:

- **Each Stop Loss**: One Stroke means a small loss;
- **Each opening**: There is a **handling fee**;
- **Holding a position overnight**: **Funding fees** may also be incurred;
- These **are accumulated** by StrokeStroke**, and then amplified** by **leverage** - G's account is in the repeated wear and tear of "small losses + handling fees + capital fees", **unknowingly shrunk by a large amount**.

**Node 1: The mistake lies in "environmental judgment" - treating shocks as trends. **

"Chasing breakthroughs" is a strategy used in **trend/breakthrough market**; if used in **shock market**, every "breakthrough" is likely to be false, and Stop Loss will naturally occur repeatedly. **The strategy is not wrong, the mistake is that it is used in the wrong environment. **

**Node 2: "The more you move, the more you lose" in the shock. **
The characteristics of the volatile market are "back and forth and no direction". In it, **frequent openings and chasing** are equivalent to **actively sending handling fees and Stop Loss** to the market. In shocks, "moving less" often saves money than "being diligent" - many veterans simply wait and see with short positions in the shocks that they can't see clearly.

**Node 3: Leverage magnifies the cost of false breakouts. **

Multiplied by the number of repetitions, the cumulative total is considerable. **Leverage doubles the cost of "high-frequency trial and error in shocks"** - This is why frequent operations with high leverage should not be used in shocks.

**Node 4: Cost is the "invisible killer". **
G may think that "my stop loss is very small every time and I don't lose much", but ignores the accumulation of **handling fees and capital fees**. Under high-frequency operation, these hidden costs can eat up a considerable part of the principal. ** Frequent trading in a volatile environment is a losing battle of attrition with "cost". **

One sentence to end: **In the volatile market, the most expensive thing is not a certain StrokeStop Loss, but "you have no direction, but you keep moving." ** When you can't see clearly, short position is also an operation.

## 1. Scene setting

Set **the same period to indicate an upward trend** (first rise and then pullback, numbers are fictitious): the price rises from 100 to 120, and then pulls back to 105. Both traders started at 100 Go Long and both made profits, but then operated their positions in completely opposite ways:

- **J: Randomly increase positions with floating profits** - The higher the price goes up, the more excited you become, adding more positions along the way and increasing leverage;
- **K: Reasonably reduce positions and lock in profits** - reduce positions in batches and pocket profits during the rising process.

## 2. Operation process

**J’s approach (increasing positions with floating profits):**

- 100 Open Long, rose to 105 → "The trend is really good, add!", add position;
- It rose to 110 → "It's still rising, add more!", added again, **even increased the leverage**;
- Rising to 115, 118 → Continue to add... Positions get bigger and bigger, **nominal exposure expands sharply**, and **average holding cost is raised all the way** (the higher you go, the more you add);
- As a result, the price rose to 120 and peaked, and **retraced to 105**: Since J's position was large and full at the high level, and the leverage was high, this wave of correction **void back all his previous floating profits**, and even **lost/approached Liquidation**.

**K’s approach (reasonably reduce positions and lock in profits):**

- 100 Open Long, rises to 110 → **Reduce part of the position and pocket part of the profit**;
- Rise to 118 → **reduce another part** to further lock in profits and lighten the position;
- The price peaked at 120, **pushed back to 105**: Because K's remaining position was already very light, this wave of correction **had little impact** on him - he **had already safely pocketed most of the profits**.

In the same market situation, J spit back the floating profit, and K took away the profit.

![C2-8 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-8-配图1.png)

## 3. Dismantling of key nodes

**Node 1: J's core error - floating profit is not "the capital to increase the position indefinitely". **
J regards "book floating profit" as "capital that can be increased indefinitely". But the floating profit has not fallen into the bag yet and will change at any time. Adding positions to higher positions means: **The exposure is getting bigger and bigger, the average cost is getting higher and higher, and the overall position is getting closer to Liquidation**. **Floating profits are not capital, they are paper numbers that have not yet been obtained** - Once there is a correction, the positions added to the high position will backfire the most.

**Node 2: J’s situation is even worse - adding more positions and increasing leverage. **
J not only increases the position, but also increases the leverage, which makes the Liquidation price closer to the current price (the higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation is, Group E caliber). So a normal callback (120 → 105) is fatal to a "large, full, and highly leveraged" position. **"Add positions with floating profits + increase leverage" exposes the account to huge risks. **

![C2-8 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-8-配图2.png)

**Node 3: K's wisdom - reducing positions is "turning uncertainty into certainty". **
The essence of K's reduction of positions in batches during the rise is to gradually turn "floating profits on the books" into "real money in pockets"**. After reducing the position, the position becomes lighter, and the taking back during the correction will be smaller. It gave up the possibility of "if the price continues to rise, the remaining positions could have earned more", in exchange for the certainty of "the profit has been obtained" - in an environment of high volatility + leverage such as contracts, this certainty is very valuable.

**Node 4: It is not impossible to add positions, but it must be "disciplined". **
Let me make it clear: it is not wrong to add positions in and of itself, what is wrong is "undisciplined and random additions". ** Adding positions in a disciplined way (pyramid style) looks like this:

- **The more you add, the less you add** (the bottom warehouse is the heaviest, and the added parts are smaller each time to prevent the center of gravity from being raised to a high position);
- **There is an upper limit** (the total position has a ceiling and will not expand infinitely);
- **Stop Loss moves up simultaneously** (after adding a position, the overall Stop Loss moves up to protect existing floating profits);
- **Do not add leverage to increase your position**.

J's position increase accounted for all negative positions (adding more and more, no upper limit, no stop loss, and increased leverage), so it was "increasing indiscriminately". **Pyramid-style disciplined adding of positions and J's kind of random adding are two different things. **

## 4. Key points of review

- **Floating profit is not "the capital to add unlimited positions"**: The floating profit on the book will change at any time. The higher the increase, the greater the exposure, the higher the cost, and the closer to Liquidation. Once the correction is made, it will all be given back or even lose money;
- **Add position with floating profit + increase leverage = high-risk combination**: The higher the leverage, the closer the Liquidation, and a normal correction may be fatal;
- **Reasonable reduction of positions = turning uncertainty into certainty**: Reduce positions in batches during the rise, pocket profits, and take back little during the correction - very valuable in a high volatility + leverage environment;
- **Add positions in a disciplined manner (pyramid style)**: add less and less, have an upper limit, Stop Loss moves up simultaneously, do not increase leverage for the purpose of adding positions - this is "adding positions", J that kind is "increasing indiscriminately";
- **There is no rigid rule of "must increase position/must reduce position"**: The core is to "control the overall risk exposure" and don't let floating profits get to your head.

![C2-8 with picture 3](/academy-img/C2-8-配图3.png)

One sentence to end: The most dangerous thought when making money is "add more, earn more". **The people who can take away the profits are often not the ones who add the most aggressive positions, but the ones who know how to slowly make money in the rising market and not let the floating profits get to their heads**.

## 5. Main points of this article

- The same period of 100→120→105 market conditions: **J Floating profit and random increase in positions (the higher the increase, the more + increase leverage) → Exposure expansion, callbacks are all given up, and even Liquidation**; **K Reasonable lightening of positions and profit locks (position reduction in batches during the rising period) → Small impact of callbacks, profits pocketed**.
- **Floating profit is not the cost of unlimited position increase**; **Floating profit increase position + leverage** will make the Liquidation price close to the current price, and a normal correction will be fatal.
- **Reasonable reduction of position = turning uncertainty into certainty**; **Addition of positions must be disciplined (pyramid style: add less and less, have an upper limit, Stop Loss moves up, and do not add leverage)**, which is different from undisciplined addition.
- ⚠️ The whole process is virtual/signaled; the core is to control the overall risk exposure; it does not constitute suggestions, predictions, and high leverage is not encouraged.

# The Cost of Emotional Trading

> Midas Academy · C2 Contract Case Library (Virtual Suggestion Review)

The biggest enemy in trading is often not the market, but your own emotions. In contracts, leverage will multiply the cost of emotional trading. This article uses a schematic case to see how trader L was dragged into a "vicious cycle" step by step by his emotions and his account shrank rapidly.

> ⚠️ The entire process is virtual/indicative, no real targets are named, no predictions of real market conditions are made, and no recommendations are constituted.

## 1. Scene setting

Trader L originally had his own plan, but on this day, **emotions took over his operations** (the process is fictitious, but extremely typical):

- Starting point: L made a stroke of a normal contract transaction, **misreading, Stop Loss** - originally this was nothing, losses are normal;
- But L** could not calmly accept this small loss of Stroke**, and his emotions started to get worse...

What happened next was a series of actions driven by emotions.

## 2. Operation process (emotionally driven vicious cycle)

**The first step·Retaliatory trading. **
The small loss in Stroke made L very unwilling: "I must make it back immediately!" So he immediately backhand, took a heavy position, and added leverage, hoping to "get it back." The result - **misread again, this time due to heavy position + high leverage, the loss was much more than the previous Stroke** (echoing F5 retaliatory trading).

**Step 2·FOMO Chase High. **
After losing two strokes in a row, L became even more panicked. At this time, he saw that another variety of ** was rising sharply, and he was afraid of "missing out on this wave" (FOMO), so he caught up with it as soon as his brain became hot. But what he was chasing was a high price that had already risen for a long time - as soon as ** caught up, the price pulled back, and he lost another Stroke** (echoing F5 to chase the rise and kill the fall).

**Step 3·Vicious cycle. **
Loss → Unwilling → Retaliatory heavy positioning → Lose more → Be more panic → FOMO chasing higher → Lose again → Even more unwilling... L fell into a **emotionally driven vicious cycle**, with increasingly chaotic operations, heavier positions, higher leverage, and **accounts shrinking rapidly in a short period of time**.

At the end of the day, L's losses were far more than the initial small stroke loss - it was emotion + leverage that turned a normal small stroke loss into a disaster. **

![C2-9 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-9-配图1.png)

## 3. Dismantling of key nodes

**Node 1: There was nothing wrong with the starting point - the fault was in the "reaction to small losses". **
L The initial small StrokeStop Loss was **completely normal** (misunderstanding is normal, C2-2). The real problem lies in his **emotional reaction** to Stroke's small loss - he is unwilling to accept it and wants to make it back immediately. **Many disasters are not caused by the Stroke loss itself, but from "the next step of losing control after the loss." **

**Node 2: Revenge trading - turning trading into gambling. **
The idea of "must make money back immediately" made L abandon all rules (heavy positions, increased leverage, and hasty entry). At this time, what he was doing was no longer trading, but gambling - the goal changed from "making the right decision" to "recovering the Stroke loss". **Orders placed with emotion are almost destined to be bad orders. **

**Node 3: Leverage amplifies every mistake made emotionally (continued from F24). **
This is the key risk of the contract: **Leverage not only magnifies profits and losses, but also magnifies the consequences of "emotional operations"**. Retaliatory heavy positioning + increased leverage magnified the loss of L's second stroke; FOMO chasing higher + leverage magnified the loss of the third stroke. **In spot trading, being emotional may make you lose money slowly; in contracts, being emotional + leverage can make you lose money quickly. **

![C2-9 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-9-配图2.png)

**Node 4: The horror of the vicious cycle - losses come from "compound interest". **
In ordinary trading, a stroke's loss is isolated. But **losses in emotional trading will be "chained"**: every loss in a stroke aggravates emotions and prompts even worse operations in the next stroke. This kind of "loss snowball" is much scarier than the loss of a single Stroke - it will drain the account in a short period of time. **

## 4. Key points of review

- **Disasters often originate from "the next out-of-control step after a loss" rather than the Stroke loss itself**: First, a small Stroke loss is normal, and the fault lies in the emotional reaction;
- **Retaliatory trading = turning trading into gambling**: Once the goal changes from "making the right decision" to "recovering losses", the order placed is almost guaranteed to be a bad order (F5);
- **FOMO chasing high = entering the market at the most dangerous position**: Chasing a high that has risen for a long time out of fear of missing out, and often pulls back (F5) just after chasing;
- ★**Leverage magnifies the cost of emotion** (continued from F24): "Emotional + Leverage" in the contract can make you explode quickly, which is far more dangerous than spot;
- **How to fight emotions**:
  - **Stop first after losing money** - leave the screen and review the Stroke (wrong judgment or execution, F7), **instead of immediately retaliate**;
  - **Rely on rules and disciplines beforehand** to combat emotions during events (F6) - for example, **set a "maximum daily loss limit", and if you lose, you will be forced to stop trading for the day**;
  - **Accepting losses is the norm**: It is far better to accept a small loss calmly than to roll into a big loss emotionally.

![C2-9 with picture 3](/academy-img/C2-9-配图3.png)

One sentence to end: **In contracts, what can destroy an account is often not a stroke of misreading a transaction, but the series of "want to get it back" impulses after the misreading. **Learning to **stop** after a loss is one of the most valuable disciplines in contract trading.

## 5. Main points of this article

- Illustrative case: L - Stroke**Stop Loss after a small loss** → **Retaliatory heavy position + Increase leverage → Lose more → FOMO chasing higher → Just after chasing, it will pull back and lose again → Vicious cycle, account shrinks rapidly**.
- The disaster comes from **"the next step of losing control after a loss"**: revenge trading (turning trading into anger), FOMO chasing highs (entering the market at the most dangerous position).
- ★**Leverage amplifies emotional costs** (continued from F24): The "emotional + leverage" in the contract is far more dangerous than the spot and can explode quickly; losses will "snowball in a chain".
- Confrontation: **Stop and review trading after a loss (non-retaliation), set a maximum daily loss limit, and rely on prior rules and discipline** (F5/F6/F7).
- ⚠️ The entire process is virtual/signaled; losses are normal, accept small losses calmly; do not constitute suggestions, do not predict, and do not encourage high leverage.

# Before Chan Theory: Build the Right Mindset

> Midas Academy · Level 3 · Module 9 Introduction to Chan Theory

**Quick overview of this article**

- Chan Theory is an analytical tool, not a prediction artifact or the Holy Grail; it improves the quality of judgment, but does not eliminate uncertainty and does not guarantee profitability.
- The correct way to study is to understand the structure and logic, rather than memorizing formulas and looking for "must rise" signals; use it as a "language" to describe the trend.
- Be wary of the tendency to deify, metaphysically, and believe in Chan Theory, and to "use it to predict and hold heavy positions"; always cooperate with risk management.
- Chan Theory** has a threshold, you need to learn it step by step**, and learn step by step in the order of concepts.

## 1. Introduction of concepts: first correct your mentality, and then learn the methods

Before really getting into the concepts of Fractal, Stroke, and Central Hub, there is a "retreat" but extremely important content that must be talked about first - **The mentality of learning Chan Theory**.

Why put mentality before technology? Because in the process of spreading, Chan Theory has been given too much exaggeration and even metaphysical color. If you go to study with wrong expectations, you will not only fail to learn well, but you may also go astray and lose money. Correcting your mentality is the prerequisite for learning Chan Theory well.

## 2. Chan Theory is an analysis tool, not a prediction tool.

This is the myth that needs to be dispelled the most. Please remember one sentence: **Chan Theory is a set of analysis tools to help you "understand and describe the trend structure". It is not a prediction artifact, nor is it the "Holy Grail" that can make a sure profit. **

- It can help you break down the messy trends into Fractal, Stroke and Central Hub in a **structured manner**, giving you a clearer understanding of the current structure.
- But it **cannot tell you what the future will definitely be**. No analytical method, including Chan Theory, can eliminate market uncertainty.
- "Learning Chan Theory will enable you to accurately copy the bottom and escape the top / make stable profits" - this kind of statement is **wrong and dangerous**. If someone promotes this, be very vigilant.

The value of any analytical tool lies in **improving the quality of your judgment** rather than giving you a "necessarily correct" answer. Chan Theory is no exception.

![C2 with picture 1](/academy-img/C2-配图1.png)

## 3. Correct learning attitude: understand the structure rather than memorize formulas

Many people take a detour when learning Chan Theory because the method is wrong. Compare the two attitudes:

**❌ Wrong learning method (be careful): **
- Memorize Chan Theory's conclusions as "mantras" without understanding the logic behind them.
- I want to find the "must rise", "must fall" and "accurate buying and selling points" signals from Chan Theory.
- Turn Chan Theory into something metaphysical and mystical, and the more you learn, the more it becomes divorced from market reality.

**✅ Correct learning method: **
- **Understand the structure and logic of each concept**: Why is Fractal so defined, why is Stroke so connected, and what does Central Hub mean.
- Treat Chan Theory as a set of "language" to describe trends, rather than a set of "fortune-telling formulas".
- Always be aware of its **limitations**: it describes structures that have already happened and are happening now, not a promise for the future.
- Everything you learn must be used in conjunction with risk management.

![C2 with picture 2](/academy-img/C2-配图2.png)

## 4. Be wary of "going crazy"

The original text of Chan Theory is obscure and has many interpretations. Various schools have formed around it in the market, many of which are overly exaggerated and even metaphysical interpretations. There are several tendencies to be especially wary of when studying:

- **Regard Chan Theory as belief**: Believe that it can explain and predict everything, and will not listen to any doubts.
- **Overcomplicating**: Digging into the minutiae, but forgetting that the fundamentals of trading are risk and probability.
- **Use it to "predict" and make heavy bets**: Treat "analyzed possibilities" as "determined future" and ignore risk management.

A healthy attitude is: **use Chan Theory as one of many analytical tools**, learn it rationally, use it critically, and always remain in awe of the market.

## 5. Step by step and accept the threshold

One final point: Chan Theory does have a **learning threshold**. Its concepts are intertwined - if you don't understand the relationship between K lines, it will be difficult to understand Fractal; if you don't understand Fractal, you won't be able to draw Stroke well; if you don't understand Stroke and Segment, you won't be able to understand Central Hub.

# Moving Average Strategy

> Midas Academy · C3 Strategy Topic Library

Moving Average strategy is the oldest and most well-known trend strategy, and it is almost every trader's first lesson. This article follows the structure of "Principle → Applicability/Failure → Usage → Advantages, Disadvantages and Risks → How to try it in Midas" to explain it thoroughly - the focus is not on "whether you can make money by using it", but on its logic and applicable boundaries**.

**Quick overview of this article**

- Moving Average strategy = **Use the Moving Average direction/cross/arrangement to determine the trend and follow the trend**; do not predict the top or bottom, but follow the established trend.
- **Applicable to unilateral trends, invalid in shocks** (Golden CrossDeath Cross has many false signals in shocks).
- Signal: **Golden Cross=Short-term Moving Average goes above the long-term (longer), Death Cross=Short-term moves below the long-term (short)**; Bullish Alignment=Price>Short>Medium>Long (strong); all are **references, not instructions**.
- The advantage is that it is simple and can catch the trend; the disadvantage is lag + many false signals + no guarantee of profit**.
- ⚠️ Midas virtual disk can be tested/backtested, and the AI ​​signal is for reference only; there are no guaranteed profit parameters and no prediction.

## 1. Strategy principles

Moving Average (MA) is the average of the closing prices of the last N periods, rolling into a line (see B1). It "smooths out" short-term fluctuations in price, allowing you to see the direction of the trend more clearly.

The core logic of the Moving Average strategy is just one sentence: **Use the direction, intersection, and arrangement of Moving Average to determine the trend, and then follow the trend. ** It does not predict tops and bottoms, it only follows the trend that has already formed.

## 2. Applicable scenarios and failure scenarios

- **Applicable to: unilateral trend market. ** When the price has a clear direction (continuously rising or falling), Moving Average can follow the trend well, filter out noise, and allow you to "stay in the trend."
- **Invalidation: Shocking market conditions. ** When the price goes back and forth in the range, Moving Average will ** frequently Golden Cross, Death Cross, and then Golden Cross ** - generating a large number of ** false signals **, allowing you to chase the rise, kill the fall, and repeatedly Stop Loss (echoing C2-5).

**In a word: Moving Average strategy is "the friend of the trend and the enemy of the shock". ** Before using it, first determine whether the current market is trending.

![C3-1 with picture 2](/academy-img/C3-1-配图2.png)

## 3. How to use (signals and rules)

Moving Average strategies commonly use three types of signals (all are **references, not buying and selling orders**):

1. **Golden Cross / Death Cross** (Double Moving Average):
   - **Golden Cross = The short-term Moving Average crosses the long-term Moving Average** from bottom to top, which is a bullish reference;
   - **Death Cross = The short-term Moving Average crosses the long-term Moving Average** from top to bottom, which is a bearish reference (the direction must not be reversed, see B2).
2. **Bull / Bearish Alignment** (Multiple Moving Average system, see B3):
   - **Bullish Alignment**: from top to bottom = price > short term > medium term > long term → strong rising structure, inclined to hold;
   - **Bearish Alignment**: From top to bottom = long term > medium term > short term > price → weak downward structure, tendency to avoid.
3. **Moving Average direction**: Moving Average is bullish upward, bearish downward, and moves flat.

In actual combat, "Golden Cross + Bullish Alignment" is often used as a structural reference for the long side, and "Death Cross + Bearish Alignment" is used as a short reference, and used in conjunction with Stop Loss.

![C3-1 with picture 1](/academy-img/C3-1-配图1.png)

## 4. Advantages, Disadvantages and Risks

**Advantages**: Simple and intuitive, widely known; can help you **seize the main rise/main decline period** and filter short-term noise; the rules are clear, easy to execute and backtest.

**Disadvantages and Risks**:

- **Lag**: Moving Average is the average of past prices. **When the cross signal appears, the price has often moved for a while** - you buy at Golden Cross and sell at Death Cross, it is destined not to be the lowest/highest point;
- **There are many false signals in shocks**: This is the biggest pain point of the Moving Average strategy (see above);
- **No guarantee of profit**: It is a trend reference. The trend may reverse at any time and may have a false breakthrough; **No Moving Average parameter can guarantee profit**.

![C3-1 with picture 3](/academy-img/C3-1-配图3.png)

# Arbitrage Strategy

> Midas Academy · C3 Strategy Topic Library

"Arbitrage" sounds beautiful - it seems like "earning the price difference without risk". But **real arbitrage is neither risk-free nor low-threshold**. This article explains the principles, thresholds and risks of arbitrage, and corrects the misunderstanding of "risk-free arbitrage". As the end of the C3 strategy library.

**Quick overview of this article**

- Arbitrage = **Neutral idea of using relevant market/variety price differences and two-leg reverse hedging to earn price differences/rates**; crypto common **Funding Rate arbitrage** (positive rate contract short charges, spot long hedging) and **period spot price difference (basis) arbitrage**.
- **Funding Rate direction**: Long positions with positive rates pay short positions, short positions with negative rates pay long positions (cannot be reversed).
- ★**Arbitrage is by no means risk-free**: Replace directional risk with a basket of risks such as **basis fluctuation, contract leg Liquidation (the most deadly), rate/spread reversal, transaction costs, liquidity**; **meager returns and high threshold**.
- ⚠️ The structure of the Midas virtual disk is understandable, and the AI ​​signal is for reference only; arbitrage is not a tutorial on making sure money, does not constitute operation advice, and does not make predictions.

## 1. Strategy principles

Arbitrage generally refers to the **neutral strategy** idea of **taking advantage of the price difference between related markets/varieties and earning the price difference** through simultaneous reverse operations (see D Dictionary, F21). Its characteristic is to try not to bet on unilateral increases or decreases, but to earn something relatively certain such as "price difference/rate". There are two common categories in encryption:

**1. Funding Rate arbitrage (neutral rate):**
Utilize the Funding Rate mechanism of Perpetual Contract (**positive rate: longs pay shorts; negative rate: shorts pay longs**, the direction cannot be reversed). Typical idea: **Hold spot long + open an equal amount of contract short** to hedge the directional risk; in the **positive rate** market, contract shorts continue to **charge** funding fees → net profit fees (echoing F21, C2-3).

**2. Futures price difference (basis) arbitrage:**
Utilize the spread between the contract price and the spot price (basis = contract price − spot price): When the basis deviates from the reasonable range and it is expected to return, earn profits from the spread return by operating the contract and spot at the same time.

## 2. Applicable scenarios and failure scenarios

- **Applicable to situations where there is a stable spread/rate, the ability to hedge both legs, and controllable costs. ** Arbitrage is suitable for participants who have funds, can operate both legs at the same time, and can strictly control costs and monitor **.
- **Invalidation/Risk Trigger**: Spread/Rate **Inverse**, Hedging Leg **Liquidation** Breaking the Hedge, **Cost Eating** Meager Gains, Liquidity Depletion - More in the next section.

![C3-10 with picture 2](/academy-img/C3-10-配图2.png)

## 3. How to use (concept and threshold)

The basic method of arbitrage (**Conceptual science, not a tutorial on making money**):

1. **Establish two hedging legs**: For example, spot long position + contract short position (in opposite directions, to hedge out the risk of rising and falling prices);
2. **Earn price difference/rate**: Net collection of capital fees under positive rate, or earn basis return;
3. ★**Strictly control costs and risks**: Handling fees, slippage, direction of funding fees, and the Liquidation risk of the hedging leg must be included in the calculation and monitoring.

**Where is the threshold? **Arbitrage** is not "just place an order and make a profit"** - it requires: sufficient funds (both legs will occupy funds), the ability to operate both legs at the same time, actuarial calculation of costs (the benefits are meager, and the costs are slightly higher and you will lose), and continuous monitoring (to prevent liquidation of the hedging leg and reversal of rates). **The bar is much higher than it seems. **

![C3-10 with picture 1](/academy-img/C3-10-配图1.png)

## 4. Advantages, Disadvantages and Risks

**Advantages**: **Neutral direction** (no betting on ups and downs, no reliance on predictions); theoretically **small fluctuations** and relatively stable returns.

**Disadvantages and risks (★Arbitrage is by no means risk-free)**: Arbitrage just replaces "directional risk" with **a basket of other risks**——

- **Basic fluctuation risk**: The spread does not return as expected, or even expands in the opposite direction;
- ★**Contract leg Liquidation risk (the most fatal)**: If the short position of the hedging contract is hit by the market market, the **hedging structure will be broken**, and it will be instantly exposed to unilateral risks;
- **Rate/spread reverse risk**: positive rate changes to negative rate (from charging to payment), price difference reverses;
- **Transaction costs**: Handling fees and slippage will **eat up the meager arbitrage returns** - thin returns are the norm for arbitrage;
- **Liquidity Risk**: One of the two legs has insufficient liquidity and cannot open/close a position in time.

**In a word: The returns from arbitrage are often meager, but the risks are real. "Risk-free arbitrage" is a misunderstanding. **

![C3-10 with picture 3](/academy-img/C3-10-配图3.png)

## 5. How to try in Midas (virtual disk)

- Understand the structure of arbitrage in Midas **virtual disk** (such as hedging two legs with long spot + short contract, net funding fee), see how it works at zero cost, and what will happen when the hedging leg Liquidation;
- Use tools to observe changes in Funding Rate and basis, and understand the sources and fluctuations of arbitrage returns (backtest/virtual ≠ real);
- Midas **AI strategy signals are for reference only**. Arbitrage involves complex two-leg operations and costs. **You must make independent judgments and be clear about thresholds and risks** and do not copy them.

# Trend Following Strategy

> Midas Academy · C3 Strategy Topic Library

Moving Average and MACD are "tools", while trend following is a **complete strategic idea** - the skeleton of many successful trading systems is trend following. This article explains its logic, approach and boundaries.

**Quick overview of this article**

- Trend following = **Follow the formed trend, do not predict the top or bottom**; the essence is "**cut losses and let profits run**"; rely on **high profit-loss ratio** to win, not rely on high winning rate.
- **Applicable to unilateral trends, invalid for shocks**; lagging at turning points (highest without selling/lowest without buying).
- Method: **Identify the trend → Enter the market with the trend (callback/breakthrough) → Move Stop Loss to follow → Leave the market if the trend goes bad**.
- Advantages include being able to take advantage of the general trend/not guessing the top and bottom/good profit-loss ratio; Disadvantages** low winning rate (need to tolerate continuous small losses) + shock and wear + lag + no guarantee of profit**.
- ⚠️ Midas virtual disk can be practiced/backtested (look at the winning rate, profit-loss ratio and retracement), and the AI ​​signal is for reference only; no prediction, no guaranteed profit.

## 1. Strategy principles

The core belief of trend following is: Once a trend is formed, it often has inertia and will continue for a period of time; instead of predicting the top or bottom, it is better to follow the trend that has already formed. **

It has a widely circulated essence: **"Cut the loss and let the profit run."** - If you are wrong, quickly Stop Loss (cut the loss), if you are right, let the trend continue to run with profits (profit amplification). Trend following does not pursue a high winning rate, but relies on the profits from a few major trends to cover multiple small losses (high profit-loss ratio).

## 2. Applicable scenarios and failure scenarios

- **Applicable to: unilateral trend market. ** When there is a clear direction (continuous rise/fall), trend following can capture the "main rise/main fall period".
- **Invalidation: Shocking market conditions. ** There is no trend to follow, and the price goes back and forth in the range. Trend following will lead to repeated entry and Stop Loss (small losses again and again), and serious wear and tear (echoing C2-5 and F12).
- **Lagging at the turning point**: Trend following naturally leaves the market after the reversal, and **will not sell at the highest and buy at the lowest**.

![C3-3 with picture 2](/academy-img/C3-3-配图2.png)

## 3. How to use (signals and rules)

Common processes for trend tracking:

1. **Identify trend**: Use high and low point structure (high points and low points rise = rise), Moving Average direction/arrangement, etc. to determine the current trend (C3-1, A7);
2. **Enter with the trend**: Do not go against the trend, do not guess the top or bottom; there are two common types of entry - **Entry with callback** (the trend will stabilize after a correction and then enter with the trend) or **Enter with the breakthrough** (enter with the trend after breaking through the key position, C3-4);
3. **Move Stop Loss to follow**: After entering the market, move the Stop Loss** in the direction of the trend** (locking part of the floating profit and giving space to the trend);
4. **Exit when the trend goes bad**: When the trend structure turns bad (falls below the moving Stop Loss/Key Moving Average, the high point no longer rises) → exit.

The whole process is the specific implementation of "**cut off loss (Stop Loss) + let profits run (move Stop Loss to follow)**".

![C3-3 with picture 1](/academy-img/C3-3-配图1.png)

## 4. Advantages, Disadvantages and Risks

**Advantages**:

- Be able to capture the main profits of the general trend;
- **No need to predict the top or bottom** (follow the trend, less psychological pressure);
- **Good profit-loss ratio** (small loss, huge profit).

**Disadvantages and Risks**:

- ★**Low winning rate**: Trend following is often "right less often and wrong more often" (many small losses), relying on a few big profits to win - **You must be able to tolerate continuous small losses**, otherwise all efforts will be wasted if you give up midway;
- **Stop Loss repeatedly during shocks**: Continuous wear and tear when there is no trend;
- **Lag**: If the entry is later than the starting point and the exit is later than the top, the head and tail will inevitably be given up;
- **No guarantee of profit**: No matter how good the trend tracking is, it will encounter continuous losses in a volatile market.

> Midas Academy · C3 Strategy Topic Library

"False breakthroughs" is the instinct of many people, but the biggest pitfall of breakthrough strategies - **false breakthroughs** - has also fooled countless people. This article explains the principles and practices of the breakthrough strategy, as well as how to deal with the unavoidable risk of false breakthroughs.

**Quick overview of this article**

- Breakthrough strategy = **After the price breaks through the key level, participate in the direction of the breakthrough** and want to seize the "starting point".
- **Applicable to post-consolidation breakthroughs/trend relay breakthroughs, and fails on the edge of shocks with frequent false breakthroughs**.
- Method: Find the key position → Wait for **effective breakthrough (closing firmly/increasing volume) and filter out false breakthroughs** → Enter the market with the trend → **Stop Loss is set on the other side of the breakthrough position**.

## 1. Strategy principles

The logic of the breakthrough strategy is: **When the price breaks through a key position (support/resistance, range boundary, previous high/previous low), it often means that the long-short balance is broken, and the price may continue to run in the direction of the breakthrough. ** (echoes F13)

Think of it as a "dam": the price is "blocked" by the upper and lower boundaries in the range; once the "dam" on a certain side is broken, the pent-up power is released, and the price may accelerate in that direction. The breakthrough strategy is to seize this "starting point".

## 2. Applicable scenarios and failure scenarios

- **Applicable to: breakthrough after consolidation and breakthrough in trend relay. ** If the price trades sideways for a long time and then breaks through, or if the price continues to break through the previous high/low during the trend, the "gold content" of the breakthrough is higher.
- **Expiration: An environment with frequent false breakthroughs, especially at the edge of a volatile market. ** The price breaks through the boundary a little bit and then **retracts** (false breakthrough), allowing those who are chasing the breakthrough to **catch at the highest/lowest price and then get trapped** (echoing C2-5).

**False breakthroughs are the inherent biggest enemy of breakthrough strategies. **
